commands.summary:
Agent definitions and chains: named roles every launch surface runs as

A definition binds a client, a model, an effort, a tool policy and a
system prompt under one name. `cast exec --as reviewer`, `cast spawn --as
reviewer`, `cast trigger add --as reviewer` and a workflow node's
`definition=reviewer` all resolve it. Definitions are workspace rows,
edited here or in Settings > Agent Library, and travel as markdown files
with frontmatter (the pi and Claude Code agents/*.md shape).

A chain runs definitions in order; each step's output feeds the next.

Examples:
  cast agent ls                              # definitions and chains
  cast agent show reviewer                   # the markdown form
  cast agent create reviewer --agent codex --model gpt-5.5 --effort high \
    --tools Read,Grep,Bash --safe -d "Reviews a diff" - <<'EOF'
  You are a senior reviewer. ...
  EOF
  cast agent import ~/.claude/agents/*.md    # bring existing roles in
  cast agent export reviewer > reviewer.md
  cast agent rm reviewer
  cast agent chain create implement --step scout:"Find code for: {task}" \
    --step planner:"Plan: {task}\n{previous}" --step worker:"Do it: {previous}"
  cast agent run implement "add retries to the sync loop"   # = cast exec --chain

commands.summary:
Show one call: title, participants, summary, action items, frames of its
video (cast call snap), and the full speaker-attributed transcript with
--transcript. Each transcript line is labeled with the reference that cites
it, so a message can name the exact words:
  cl-42           # in a message: the call, as a live pill (a card alone on its line)
  cl-42:15-25     # in a message: lines 15 to 25, embedded alone on a line
  cast call cl-42 15:25   # print just those lines
  cast call cl-42@12:34   # the lines being said at 12m34s
and a link can too:
  https://codecast.sh/calls/<id>?turns=<from>-<to>   # those lines, selected
  https://codecast.sh/calls/<id>?part=summary        # the summary
  https://codecast.sh/calls/<id>?part=action-<n>     # action item n (from 1)

cast call hold <duration>|off   # from a session a live huddle feeds: hold
                                # the room's words for a stretch of work

A recorded call has video, and snap pulls a frame of it as a PNG you can open
(`cast call snap --help` for this part alone):
  cast call snap cl-42:15         # the moment line 15 was said (or: snap cl-42 15)
  cast call snap cl-42@12:34      # 12m34s into the call (also @754s, @754 and @12m34s)
  cast call snap cl-42:15-25      # frames across lines 15 to 25 (where the screen changed)
  cast call snap cl-42:15 --crop top-left   # a quarter of the frame at full size, for small text
  cast call snap cl-42            # right now, while the call records
A frame shows the shared screen from its own full-resolution file whenever one was
recorded, else the room (--composite prefers the room, and says so where only a share
was recorded). Each frame prints with the line being said and its citation: cl-42@12:34
alone on a line in a message renders as that same picture for anyone who can read the
call. --json gives each frame's path, kind (screen or composite) and what it shows; a
refusal gives its code and a `try` list of the commands that will work. `cast call <id>`
says what was recorded and marks each filmed line with ▸. Each frame prints its size: a
wide one is shrunk before a model reads it, so for small text on a shared screen take
part of it (--crop) or all of it in overlapping tiles (--tiles 2x1). Times may carry a
fraction (cl-42@2:30.5). --share uploads frames as public images, only for readers
outside codecast, and only by whoever recorded the call, a team admin, or the person
whose screen it shows; the room is told, and deleting the recording deletes them.
The stretch still being recorded has only its live picture, for people in the call,
until Record is stopped; stretches already saved can be snapped at once. Needs ffmpeg.

flags.description: Machine-readable output (a call always includes segments; a snap gives frames, or {error, code, try})
With `hold`: the fed session (default: the current one)
With `snap`: only a shared screen will do; refuse (code no_screen) where none was recorded
With `snap`: prefer the room view (faces and the share as everyone saw it)
With `snap`: a .png/.jpg file, or a directory (default: a private scratch directory)
With `snap` on a line range: at most this many frames (default 8, up to 50)

With `snap`: only part of each frame, at full resolution: top, bottom, left, right, top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, center, or x,y,w,h in pixels or percent (its own file, named by the part, beside any whole frame)
With `snap`: each frame also as tiles at full resolution, columns x rows (2x2 writes _tl, _tr, _bl, _br), each reaching a little past its neighbours so a line on a seam is whole in one

With `snap`: upload each frame as a public image anyone with its link can open; only for readers outside codecast, and only by whoever recorded the call, a team admin, or the person whose screen it shows (cite cl-42@12:34 for everyone else)

commands.summary:
Add an owner to a session — a team member responsible for steering it

A session has a SET of owners: it can sit in several teammates' inboxes at
once, and each owner gets a notification when they're added. `own` ADDS an
owner without displacing the existing ones (use `disown` to remove one).

An owner is distinct from whose account RUNS the session, and from which
DEVICE it runs on — all three move independently. An agent account (e.g. a
bot on a shared machine) can park a session on a human reviewer; it then
surfaces in the OWNER's inbox (web NEEDS INPUT + cast sessions/feed) marked
with who runs it. Owners reply with cast send or the web composer.

Ownership decides whose inbox it is in. A session you run but own no part
of leaves your inbox and stops notifying you, whatever state it is in; name
its id to read it anyway. An owned session stays in the owner's inbox with
no recency limit, and a handoff clears a dismiss, stash or snooze so it
lands where they can see it.

You can own any session you can see in the feed (your own, or one shared
with a team you're in). Scripts should pass an exact email.

Examples:
  cast own jx7c6zk jason@example.com   # hand off to a teammate (notifies them)
  cast own jason@example.com           # …hand off the CURRENT session
  cast own jx7c6zk                     # claim it yourself
  cast owners jx7c6zk                  # who owns it
  cast disown jx7c6zk                  # step off it yourself
  cast disown jx7c6zk --all            # clear every owner

commands.summary:
Explore sessions — three independent axes:

  QUERY (which sessions): session ids, --state, --label, --team / -m … narrow the set
  CONTENT: work state by default (grouped NEEDS INPUT → DONE → WORKING → DORMANT → IDLE),
           or --messages for conversation messages
  LIVENESS: a one-shot snapshot, or -w to stream changes live

States answer WHO ACTS NEXT, matching the web inbox. NEEDS INPUT = a human must unblock it
(open question, permission prompt, dead with output, or a finished turn nobody classified).
DONE = the agent delivered (`cast state --status done`); review at leisure. WORKING = the
agent is producing now. DORMANT = a machine wakes it (a declared `cast state --status
dormant`, an open background task/Monitor, or an armed trigger into it) — nothing is yours
until then. IDLE = blank sessions. --json swaps any view to JSON.

Watch mode (-w) is the monitoring primitive: it prints NOTHING until something changes,
then one line per change — safe to run in the background and wake on output. With --json
each line is one NDJSON event:
  {"ts":…,"event":"new"|"transition"|"gone","id":…,"title":…,"from":…,"to":…,"label":…}
new = session entered the watched set · transition = work_state changed · gone = left
the set (stopped matching --state, or dismissed). Event states use underscores
("needs_input"); the --state flag accepts either form.

Orchestrate a fleet: spawn workers under a label, watch that label, act when a worker
flips to done (finished) or needs_input (blocked); dormant means parked, not blocked:
  cast spawn --label fleet "task A" "task B"
  cast sessions --label fleet -w --json   # → {"event":"transition","to":"done",…}
  cast read <id>  /  cast send <id> "next step"

Examples:
  cast sessions                  # state snapshot of your sessions
  cast sessions -w               # stream state changes live
  cast sessions jx7abc jx7def -w # watch an explicit set of sessions
  cast sessions --label fleet -w --json   # NDJSON events for one label's sessions
  cast sessions --state needs-input   # only what's waiting on you
  cast sessions --team -w        # stream the whole team's state changes
  cast sessions --messages -w    # follow messages across your live sessions
  cast sessions jx7abc --messages -w  # …focused on one session
  cast sessions jx7abc --messages     # one session's recent messages
  cast sessions --labels         # my labels with session counts (current project)
  cast sessions --labels -g      # …across all projects
  cast sessions --by-label -a    # group all sessions by label

The text renders pinned above the composer in the dashboard and on the inbox
card, so the human sees the situation the moment they open the session instead
of reading back through it. First line: what this session is working on, plain
and unlabeled. You own it: rewrite it whenever the answer changes, and clear it
when it stops being true. The dashboard shows how many messages have passed
since you wrote it, so a stale state is visible as stale.

Subcommands:
  cast state                     Print the pinned state of this session
  cast state "<text>"            Pin (or replace) the state
  cast state clear               Remove it
  cast state show <session>      Print another session's state

--status is your answer to WHO ACTS NEXT, and it decides where the session
files in the inbox when your turn ends:
  working   still moving (default)
  blocked   a human must act to unblock you            → Needs Input
  done      delivered; nothing stalled, review at leisure → Done
  dormant   a machine wakes you — name the wake in the text → Dormant
done and dormant cover exactly the turn that declares them: after the next
wake, declare again or the session returns to Needs Input.

Examples:
  cast state --status dormant "Waiting on CI run 8841 — tr-42 re-checks at 3pm"
  cast state --status blocked - <<'EOF'
  Migrating the sync layer to wake signatures
  Status: rewrite done, tests green
  Blocked: needs a prod key before the last check
  EOF
  cast state --status done "Shipped — all four fixes verified in the browser"
  cast state clear               # the state no longer holds

Show the active Claude account's usage-limit windows (5h session, 7d) and what a limit hit means for sessions here

Read and write local markdown vaults (the web app calls this Files)

A vault is a directory of markdown you registered. The daemon serves it
to the web app's Files page over its local 127.0.0.1 bridge; these
commands read and write the same files directly, so a note you change
here shows up in an open browser tab within a second. Registration is
per-device and the files never leave this machine.

Managing the list of vaults:
  cast vault add ~/notes
  cast vault add ~/work/wiki --name Wiki
  cast vault ls
  cast vault mirror ~/notes --on   # let other devices read it
  cast vault forget ~/notes        # unregister; the files stay

Working on notes — the loop an agent runs:
  cast vault search 'tag:health sleep'      # find the note
  cast vault cat Sleep                      # read it
  cast vault grep 'bed at' --path 'Areas/**'  # find the exact line
  cast vault edit Sleep --old 'bed at 11' --new 'bed at 10'
  cast vault links Sleep                    # what points here
  cast vault open Sleep                     # a link for the human

Paths: every command takes a vault-relative path OR the bare name a
[[wiki link]] would use, resolved by the same rules the app uses. A name
matching several notes errors and lists them.

Vaults: --vault <id|name|dir> picks one. Without it, commands use the
vault the current directory is inside — so inside a project you can just
say `cast vault cat <note>`. With a single registered vault anywhere,
that one is used.

Machine-readable: every read command takes --json.

Exit codes: 0 ok · 1 not found · 2 ambiguous (name or vault matched
several) · 3 the vault's directory is unreachable
